job: Fresh graduate in computing and engineering
name: Bilal Varga

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Hello, and thanks for making time. I'm a senior field researcher with the Work Futures Panel. We're an independent group, with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government, and we're not selling anything. What you tell me stays confidential, so you can say what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. To start, tell me about a normal day right now, in your job hunt, your first job or your studies.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm a junior support engineer at a start-up in Bristol that makes software for smart energy meters. I've been there three months. My day is answering tickets from utility companies, reproducing their problems, and passing the nasty ones to the developers. I use an AI assistant for nearly everything: drafting replies, reading logs, explaining old code. I did computer engineering, passed with an average mark, no internship, and I'm in a flat with three other people. My mum is a nurse and she's proud, but she can't help me with money. The loan is big and my savings would cover about three weeks.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say fine, more of the same. At work I'd tell my boss Ines that the tools are good for my tickets but nobody's replaced. To friends I'd say it's the dot-com thing again, big noise and then a steady grind. Online I'd say the useful bits are real and the hype is silly, and then I'd go back to building things.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Between us, it means I'm still on a low wage, in a shared flat, with a loan. The AI tools save me an hour a day, but the start-up has only eleven months of cash, which has nothing to do with AI. If the funding doesn't come, I'm out whatever the tech does. So I'd say I'm a bit uneasy, not afraid.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep using the tools hard, because they make me faster than people with more experience. I'd keep building my side project, a small bot that sorts landlord complaints for tenant groups. I'd try to get three more months of savings and I'd apply quietly to a couple of bigger firms as insurance. I'd also join the local engineers' union branch because they run free training.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It feels okay. Dull maybe, but dull is safe. The only real nerves are about the start-up's money.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said the start-up has eleven months of cash. How do you know that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ines said it at an all-hands meeting, very casually, like it was good news. I did the sums with the number of staff and it's closer to nine months if they hire. I keep an eye on the careers page now, which sounds paranoid but isn't. I'd rather be early than caught.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What's the side project, and would it earn anything?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It's a little tool that reads tenants' emails to landlords and sorts them by urgency, like damp or no heating. A tenants' group in Bristol uses it for free. If I charged £5 a month per group I might get £200 a month in a year. That would be real money for me, so I haven't ruled it out.

say: I'd say the useful bits are **real** and the hype is silly.
I'd tell Ines (my boss) the tools help my tickets but nobody's **replaced**.
think: The tools save me an **hour** a day, but the start-up only has months of cash.
I'm **uneasy**, not afraid, because funding matters more than the technology.
do: Keep using AI tools **hard** to stay faster than experienced colleagues.
Build my **side project** for tenant groups towards £200 a month.
Apply quietly to a couple of bigger **firms** as insurance.
feel: Fine and a bit **dull**, with nerves only about the start-up's money.
S0.quote: I'd rather be early than caught.
fieldNote: His unease is about **funding**, and he has done the arithmetic himself.
He treats AI as a daily tool and is quietly building income of his own.
Applying elsewhere is insurance, not disloyalty.

steps.text: Keep using the AI assistant for ticket replies and log reading
Charge tenant groups £5 a month for the email sorting tool
Apply quietly to two bigger Bristol firms
Save three extra months of rent

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's good and bad, the way every big change is. At work I'd tell Ines we should move before the customers do: put an AI front line on tickets and have humans handle the hard ones. To friends I'd say learn the tools, because the person who knows the tools replaces the person who doesn't. Online I'd say the unions and governments need to catch up with rules for how firms use this.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, it means my job as it is gets smaller. Answering tickets is exactly the sort of work that moves to software. But I'm the one in the team who can build the system that does it. So I think my job turns into the one watching the machine, which is fine if there's still a place for me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd pitch Ines a project to build the AI ticket assistant myself, with me as the owner. I'd learn more about how the models are built and tested, through an online course in my evenings. I'd keep the side project going and try to charge for it. And I'd save as much as I can, since being early doesn't help if the firm goes bust.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It feels exciting and a bit scary. Mostly I'm impatient, because I want to get ahead of it before the other graduates do.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would the pitch to Ines sound like?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Something like, we get four hundred tickets a week, and sixty per cent are the same ten problems. Let me build an assistant that answers those and flags the rest, and I'll track how often it's wrong. It saves the firm a hire it can't afford. I'd put numbers on it, because Ines likes numbers.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Does it bother you that you'd be building the thing that replaces your own role?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A little. But if I don't, somebody else will, and a vendor will sell it to us for more. I'd rather be the person who understands it and owns it. I do worry about the support colleagues, like Sam (a colleague on the ticket desk) who answers phones and isn't going to retrain.

say: I'd tell Ines (my boss) to put an AI **front line** on tickets, with humans on hard cases.
I'd say governments need **rules** for how firms use AI.

fieldNote: He reframes exposure as **opportunity**, which matches his adaptive profile.

steps.text: Pitch Ines a plan to build an AI assistant for common tickets
Take an evening course on testing language models
Start charging for the tenant email sorting tool
Save every spare pound towards three months of rent

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say that's too fast for a normal system to cope with, and anyone who says they're ready is lying. At work I'd ask Ines straight whether the company survives it. To friends I'd say get cash and get skills in things that need a body. Online I'd shout for a universal basic income and for slowing down the rollout.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Between us, I'm scared. It's thinking work that goes first, and my degree is exactly that. Even with the AI skills I have, a firm needs far fewer people when an AGI can do the work. I'd have maybe eighteen months of work left in the thinking world, and I owe a lot.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd do two things at once. First, push the side income hard, selling the tenant tool and anything else I can build, so I own something. Second, retrain for something hands-on: I like electronics, so I'd look at a lab technician course or a solar installer apprenticeship. I'd move to my cousin's place in Cardiff if rent got impossible, and I'd go to every protest about basic income.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It feels like a sprint where nobody told me the distance. I'm adrenalised more than frozen, but I know that can stop fast.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said adrenalised rather than frozen. What do you think makes the difference?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I've always tried new things quickly. When I picked up coding at fifteen, it was because I got bored. So I move fast, but I also crash fast. The real danger is a bad month: if the rent's due and I've got nothing, the speed is no use.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who would you turn to if you hit that bad month?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My cousin Rafi (his cousin) in Cardiff. He's got a spare room and he's a plumber, so he'd be okay. My mum would help if she could, but she's got her own bills. I'd tell my cousin early, not at the last minute.

say: I'd say no normal system can cope, and ask Ines if the **company** survives.
I'd shout for a **basic income** and slower rollout.
think: Thinking work goes first and my **degree** is exactly that.
I'd have maybe **eighteen months** of work left in the thinking world.

feel: Like a **sprint** with no distance told, adrenalised rather than frozen.
S2.quote: I move fast, but I also crash fast.
fieldNote: Adaptability gives him **momentum** and a two-track plan, but he spots its limits himself.
The cousin in Cardiff is a real fallback, which his peers often lack.
He is anxious, not alarmed, because he still feels some control.

steps.text: Sell the tenant tool to ten more groups and build a second product
Apply for a solar installer apprenticeship near Bristol
Ask my cousin Rafi in Cardiff for his spare room if rent bites
Join marches calling for a basic income

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is enough to get ready, if you start now. At work I'd tell Ines to train the whole team on the tools this year. To friends I'd say start something of your own, even small. Online I'd back training funds and an eye on how firms use AI.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly it feels like an opportunity with a trapdoor. I could be in a good spot by 2031, with an owned product and real savings. But the trapdoor is that the rest of my life, rent and the loan, runs on a clock too. I'd want to be less dependent on a single employer.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd aim to leave support for an engineering role within two years, ideally at a firm that builds AI systems, not just buys them. I'd grow the side project into something that earns £500 a month. I'd save for a deposit on a small flat, though that depends on the loan. And I'd volunteer teaching AI tools to a community centre, because teaching makes me learn.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It feels good, like there's a game and I know the rules. I still have flickers of dread, but they pass.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why teach at a community centre?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because I learn the tools best when I'm explaining them to somebody who's afraid of them. Also, I'd meet people, and some of them run businesses that need help. Half of my best ideas came from sitting beside someone who didn't get it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said the rest of your life runs on a clock. Which part?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The loan, and my mum's retirement. She's fifty-one and has a bad back from nursing, and I know I'll be expected to help eventually. So the five years isn't only about my career, it's about being someone who can catch her if she needs it.

I'd say start something of your **own**, even small.
think: It's an opportunity with a **trapdoor**, because rent and the loan run on a clock.

S3.quote: Half of my best ideas came from sitting beside someone who didn't get it.
fieldNote: His long-term plan includes his **mother's** future, which adds pressure and meaning.
He learns by teaching, which fits his curious style.

steps.text: Apply for an AI engineering role within two years
Grow the tenant tool to £500 a month
Teach a weekly AI tools class at the community centre
Start a fund to help my mum when her back gets worse

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is a gift. At work I'd say let's design the team for 2036 now. To friends I'd say you'll live in a different world, so be curious. Online I'd say governments should make training free and keep an eye on who owns the AI.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Between us, I'm pretty calm. If I keep learning, I should be fine, and ten years is long enough to clear the loan, build savings and maybe a business. The thing I keep thinking about is who owns the machines, because if it's three companies, nobody else gets much. That's my real worry, more than my job.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep building the side project into a real small company, maybe with a partner. I'd move into more senior engineering work as fast as I can. I'd save for a deposit and help my mum. And I'd get involved in a group that argues for sharing the gains of AI, because I think that's the real fight.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It feels hopeful. I'm still twenty-two, with a lot of runway. I can imagine being someone who helped people through this instead of being flattened by it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would sharing the gains look like to you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A public fund, or a tax on the profits, that pays for training and a basic income. I'm not an economist, so I'd be happy for people who are to design it. What I'd do is show up, write to my representative, and use my skills to build tools for the groups that campaign.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What could knock your hopeful picture over?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, getting sick, or the start-up collapsing in the next year and me being out of work during a hiring freeze. Ten years is long, but the first two are what break people. I need to get through them with a little money and a decent reference.

say: I'd say ten years is a **gift** and governments should make training free.
I'd tell colleagues to design the team for **2036** now.
think: I'm pretty **calm** if I keep learning, but worry about who owns the machines.
Ten years is long enough to clear the **loan** and build savings.
do: Build the side project into a **small company**, maybe with a partner.
Move into more **senior** engineering work as fast as I can.
Join a group arguing for **sharing** the gains of AI.
feel: Hopeful, able to imagine helping people through this rather than being **flattened**.
S4.quote: Ten years is long, but the first two are what break people.
fieldNote: His calm rests on **skills** and runway, while he names the early-years risk.
His politics emerge as concern for who owns the machines.

steps.text: Turn the tenant tool into a small registered company
Move into senior engineering work within five years
Write to my representative and volunteer for a campaign group
Save a house deposit and a fund to help my mum

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The two-year one, because the rent doesn't wait for policy. I can move fast, but I can't beat a deadline that short with no savings. What would help is a safety net that kicks in quickly, retraining that pays something, and a rule that lets a firm keep humans on while they adjust.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Only that the people who say young graduates should just learn AI forget that most of us have no money to fall back on. Speed is a skill, and I have it, but I'd like it to be a choice. I'd like the ground under me to be firm enough to try things.

headlineQuote: Speed is a skill, and I have it, but I'd like it to be a choice.
portrait: Bilal is a 22-year-old computer engineering graduate in a junior **support engineer** job at a Bristol energy software start-up.
He is progressive and adaptive: he uses AI every day and builds a side project for tenant groups.
His money is thin, with heavy debt, a shared flat and a mother who is a **nurse**.
Fast change makes him anxious rather than frozen, and ten years makes him calm.
He worries as much about who owns the machines as about his own job.
biggestWorry: The **two-year** picture, because rent will not wait and he has almost no savings.
whatWouldHelp: A fast **safety net**, paid retraining, and a rule that keeps humans in work while firms adjust.
